text:
Dear Dr. Reynolds,

Thank you for agreeing to see this 16-year-old young man for further evaluation of progressive skeletal and soft tissue changes that first began when he was nine years old.

Over the past several years, he has suffered from persistent, deep aching and significant discomfort across his thighs and trunk. On examination, palpable, hard masses consistent with extra-skeletal bone formation are clearly identifiable embedded within the deep skeletal muscle of his right quadriceps and left paraspinal region. Foot inspection reveals a bilateral lateral angulation of the first metatarsophalangeal joints, and both great toes appear disproportionately elongated relative to the adjacent digits.

His general physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. Motor power is preserved at 5/5 in all four limbs, deep tendon reflexes are symmetric, and joint range of motion elsewhere is completely normal. He is a high school student who lives with both parents, and there is no family history of inherited bone pathology. He currently takes only occasional acetaminophen for symptom relief.

Recent blood investigations showed a distinctly increased serum alkaline phosphatase level. Importantly, his total calcium was normal, serum phosphorus levels were well within the reference range, and C-reactive protein was not elevated.

I would be very grateful for your comprehensive assessment of these clinical and laboratory findings and your guidance on how best to investigate and manage his condition moving forward.

Kind regards,

Dr. Julian Ward
Department of Pediatrics, Oakridge Community Hospital
